key points:
Why Language Models Hallucinate
 * Language models are incentivized to guess when they don't know the answer, as training gives a "thumbs up" for correct answers and a "thumbs down" for everything else, including "I don't know" answers [02:00].
 * The training and evaluation procedures create a "natural statistical pressure" for models to hallucinate [03:09].
 * There's no penalty for wrong answers, and the models are always in "test-taking mode" [11:43].
Confidence and Self-Certainty
 * Language models have an internal sense of confidence in their answers. Consistency in answers to the same question indicates their certainty [05:38].
 * Models can be trained using their own confidence as a reward signal, a method called "reinforcement learning from internal feedback" [05:54].
The Role of Pre-Training and Post-Training
 * Base models will always have hallucinations because they're not trained to eliminate them [11:51].
 * Post-training helps reduce hallucinations but doesn't eliminate them completely [09:36].
Solutions to Hallucinations
 * The solution is to reward models for expressing uncertainty, similar to how humans get social credit for admitting they don't know something [13:51].
 * Updating benchmarks to reward expressions of uncertainty could significantly reduce hallucinations, as most popular benchmarks use binary grading [14:51].
Conclusion
 * The video suggests we've been approaching the problem from the wrong angle. A minor tweak in the training process could lead to a significant improvement [18:14].
 * This new approach could be a breakthrough, although it might mean we see more "I don't know" answers from language models [16:31].

comments.author: @martinjackson7111
comments.text: Not sure I would use the word SOLVED.  If I have a model that knows 50% of the answers on a benchmark and to simplify the analysis there are only 2 answers one right and one wrong.  Currently it would get 75% (the 50% it knows and the 50% of 50% it guesses).  If we change the benchmark to not penalise IDK but do penalise wrong answers (i.e. -1)  then it would score 50% for what it knows and 0% for saying IDK, so overall= 50%;  if it guessed it would get 50% for what it knows and (-25% for wrong guesses and +25 for correct guesses) = also 50% in total.  So now the model only scores 50% which accurately reflects the model's performance, but that is 25% lower than what is was scoring on the existing benchmarks.  So in effect we haven't solved hallucinations we have just made the benchmark more accurately reflect the models real-world performance - i.e. it still isn't any better than it was and it isn't getting any closer to AGI or whatever.  In the real-world the cost of a wrong answer could be much worse that the reward for a correct answer.  For example if in our case above if the wrong guess means that next week you are going to need to go to hospital to have painful surgery it would probably be better for you if it says IDK - so you can get a second or third opinion.  So in this case you might apply a weighting factor - let's say 10:1.  So now we get 50% for those it knows are right but then ( 25 -25*10)/10 = -22.5% for guessing - so now our overall benchmark score is just 27.5%.   I think that this is what reports like the MIT survey with 95% non-adoption rates are starting to show , i.e.  the current benchmark performance numbers are skewed to reward guessing, but in real scenarios where the downside is worse than IDK then the models are not viable.  Currently I think the high benchmark scores of these models are massively hyped up because they accept hallucinations with no downside. Remove hallucinations and create more non-binary weighted benchmarks to represent real-world scenarios, and we will see the true performance of these models  - so I cannot see the AI companies going that way any time soon.

comments.text: The problem with hallucinations isn’t just that training rewards guessing or allows “I don’t know” responses—it’s that artificial intelligence faces no negative consequences for being wrong. This evolutionary pressure forged strong incentives for accuracy, caution, and effective uncertainty management: when not knowing was safer than making a reckless guess. Artificial systems, lacking those stakes, optimize for fluency and plausibility rather than truth, which makes confident but incorrect answers far more common.

comments.author: @anjuro
comments.text:
I find this explanation kind of bizarre. Before LLMs we had smaller more domain specific neural networks, like classification models. For example, there are many toy examples about building a model that can take an input as an image and determine which of a finite set of classes (e.g. cat, dog, horse etc.) describes the image. The 2 basic evaluation criteria in training such a model are the confidence and getting the right answer. The confidence is determined from the distribution of the activation on the output layer of the network (So if the weights are something like 0.01, 0.01, 0.098 the model is very confident that class 3 is the answer, or to put it another way, it can clearly distinguish the classes, conversely weights like 0.45, 0.55, 0.05 would indicate that the model cannot tell classes 1 and 2 apart very well, the model is likely not able to classify them reliably). If either criteria is missing we would say that the model does not work reliably, either the architecture needs to be tweaked or the data is weak or more training is needed. This is such a basic concept that I find it hard to believe the people making LLMs did not know about it, ultimately an LLM model still just picks 1 of the tokens from the embedding space and has a "confidence" for said token. 

The only explanation that makes sense to me is that the equivalency breaks with LLMs. Predicting the next token in a text is not deterministic, there will be points where multiple words fit, that is why we have temperature controls for LLMs, to sample from a larger space than just 1 "best" most confident answer. Uncertainty in the result is sort of baked into the inference architecture. That inherently means even with infinite training, the model can never be confident, next token prediction does not have a deterministic answer in general. I suppose this is partly why LLMs didn't really work until transformer architecture was invented, but even that does not foundationally fix the issue of confidence. Now of course, some sentences do have a clear right answer, so you can still sort of play the same game as before where high confidence is seen as an evaluation criterion for if the model is working, but to me its kinda unclear how you handle the dichotomy of sentences that cannot be confident (which I imagine is the vast majority) and sentences that can.

I think that the problem is the next-token prediction paradigm itself, and no amount of "duct tape" will fix it, the model prediction needs to move furtheer back into the latent space and possibly generate on the "idea" level instead of the "word snippet" level (which is what tokens are right now), then I think we could wrestle back some of that confidence.
